sourceCheck: Verified on 2026-10-08: the [official exam page](https://training.linuxfoundation.org/certification/certified-kubernetes-security-specialist/) names Certified Kubernetes Security Specialist (CKS), and both it and the [FAQ](https://docs.linuxfoundation.org/tc-docs/certification/faq-cka-ckad-cks) specify Kubernetes v1.35. The retained deck pin is upstream Kubernetes v1.35. The exam page's 26 unnumbered competencies match the supplied definition. Its weights are Cluster Setup 15%, Cluster Hardening 15%, System Hardening 10%, Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20%, Supply Chain Security 20%, and Monitoring, Logging and Runtime Security 20%. Section numbers and competency groupings are deck-defined. The [curriculum repository](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum) and linked [CKS_Curriculum v1.34.pdf](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/master/CKS_Curriculum%20v1.34.pdf) were opened: the filename and link were readable, but the PDF body was unreadable through the available renderer and raw routes. PDF wording and weight agreement therefore remain unverified. Its v1.34 artifact label is distinct from the exam environment version. The [CKS README](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/blob/master/cks/README.md) publishes 10%, 15%, 15%, 20%, 20%, 20%, conflicting for Cluster Setup and System Hardening; this deck follows the exam page. The verification date is not a curriculum effective date. Specified Kubernetes and maintainer sources, relevant subsections, and feature notices were read. Pinned v1.35 documentation is a static snapshot. AppArmor's structured API, seccomp, seccompDefault, Pod Security Admission, and ValidatingAdmissionPolicy are stable; AppArmor annotations are deprecated rather than removed. Baseline includes the applicable probe and lifecycle-hook host restriction introduced in v1.34. Permanent ServiceAccount token autogeneration is obsolete, while manual indefinite tokens remain possible. KMS v1 and PodSecurityPolicy are excluded; PodSecurityPolicy was removed in v1.25. User namespaces, MutatingAdmissionPolicy, and fine-grained kubelet authorization are excluded where their v1.35 behavior is beta. The [v1.36 release post](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/04/22/kubernetes-v1-36-release/) confirms later stable graduations and Ingress NGINX retirement on March 24, 2026; those graduations do not change this pin, and retirement of that controller does not retire the Ingress API. Signed Kubernetes artifact publication is labeled beta, so cards assume a published artifact and make no universal asset-availability claim. Documented signing identities may change. Kubesec's legacy profile annotations and KubeLinter's experimental keyless-signing example are stale; pinned Kubernetes fields and current Sigstore guidance take precedence. No external project release pin is needed by the plan, and maintainer examples do not establish exam-installed tools. Metadata/RBAC and dedicated-etcd-CA cards draw security consequences from the checklist's separate endpoint and trust-root recommendations.

cards.statement: With enforcement enabled, ingress isolation alone leaves a Pod's NetworkPolicy egress access unrestricted.
cards.explanation: Ingress isolation controls incoming connections; outgoing connections need a separate egress restriction.

cards.statement: An enforcing plugin gives a later restrictive NetworkPolicy priority over an earlier broad allowance.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy allowances accumulate, so an existing broad allowance survives a more restrictive policy.
cards.misconception: Newer restrictive policies override older allowances.

cards.statement: With enforcement enabled, a destination's ingress allowance overrides its source Pod's egress denial.
cards.explanation: A Pod connection needs permission at both isolated ends; destination ingress permission leaves source egress restrictions intact.
cards.misconception: Destination ingress permission overrides source egress isolation.

cards.statement: A Pod under enforced default-deny egress needs an allowance to reach the cluster DNS service.
cards.explanation: Default-deny egress blocks DNS traffic; workloads need a permitted path to cluster DNS.

cards.statement: An enforced NetworkPolicy allowing TCP port 443 verifies the peer's TLS certificate.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy filters connections; another control needs to validate TLS certificates.
cards.misconception: Permitting the HTTPS port validates peer certificates.

cards.statement: NetworkPolicy ingress isolation permits traffic from the selected Pod's resident node.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy exempts ingress from the Pod's local node, leaving that node outside this isolation boundary.

cards.statement: An enforcing plugin's ICMP filtering under default-deny NetworkPolicy depends on its implementation.
cards.explanation: NetworkPolicy leaves ICMP handling undefined; plugins may permit or drop it.

cards.statement: NetworkPolicy prescribes immediate closure of established TCP sessions after a policy denies their traffic.
cards.explanation: The network plugin determines whether policy changes affect established connections.
cards.misconception: Policy changes prescribe immediate session termination.

cards.statement: Once a plugin handles a NetworkPolicy, it enforces that Pod's isolation for init containers too.
cards.explanation: Processed NetworkPolicy isolation covers init containers because they share their Pod's network.

cards.statement: The API server confirms dataplane enforcement when it accepts a new NetworkPolicy.
cards.explanation: The Kubernetes API exposes no enforcement-readiness signal; plugin processing can lag.
cards.misconception: API acceptance confirms installed network enforcement.

cards.statement: A passing kube-bench assessment can establish the security of an application's software dependencies.
cards.explanation: kube-bench assesses Kubernetes configuration; application dependency vulnerabilities need a separate assessment.
cards.misconception: Passing configuration checks establishes dependency security.

cards.statement: A kube-bench FAIL result can reflect a check execution error rather than a configuration mismatch.
cards.explanation: Read kube-bench's remediation output to distinguish a configuration failure from an error that prevented checking.

cards.statement: A kube-bench WARN result establishes that the assessed setting complies with the benchmark.
cards.explanation: WARN needs further assessment, such as a manual check, before administrators determine compliance.
cards.misconception: WARN is a weaker PASS.

cards.statement: A kube-bench Job on a worker assesses the local host configuration available to that Job.
cards.explanation: kube-bench inspects host processes and files; checking a control-plane node requires access to that node.

cards.statement: Administrators can identify a compatible CIS Benchmark by matching its number to the Kubernetes minor.
cards.explanation: CIS and Kubernetes use separate version schemes; select a benchmark with documented coverage for the cluster.
cards.misconception: Benchmark numbers track Kubernetes minor versions.

cards.statement: In the standard Ingress TLS model, the controller encrypts its connection to backend Pods.
cards.explanation: Standard Ingress TLS ends at the ingress point; backend transport encryption needs separate controller configuration.
cards.misconception: Ingress TLS encrypts the backend connection.

cards.statement: A TLS-enabled Ingress associates its TLS hostnames with matching host rules.
cards.explanation: Matching TLS and rule hosts connects the configured encrypted hostname to its intended route.

cards.statement: An SNI-enabled Ingress controller shares one TLS port between several configured hostnames.
cards.explanation: Controller SNI support selects the configured TLS host using the hostname in the client's handshake.

cards.statement: The Ingress API specifies a uniform set of TLS features for Ingress controllers.
cards.explanation: Controllers offer different TLS features; verify the chosen controller's support before depending on an option.
cards.misconception: Ingress TLS features are portable across controllers.

cards.statement: An Ingress rule with its host omitted can expose a backend through unintended hostnames.
cards.explanation: A hostless rule routes matching paths regardless of the request hostname, broadening backend exposure.

cards.statement: API server RBAC governs a Pod's permission to read the node metadata API.
cards.explanation: Node metadata uses a separate endpoint; administrators filter workload network access to protect it.
cards.misconception: Kubernetes RBAC covers node metadata requests.

cards.statement: Mutual TLS on a publicly reachable etcd endpoint can provide the recommended control-plane network isolation.
cards.explanation: etcd needs restricted network exposure as well as mutual TLS; transport authentication leaves public reachability intact.
cards.misconception: Mutual TLS supplies network isolation for public etcd.

cards.statement: Administrators restrict kubelet API network exposure separately from Kubernetes API server exposure.
cards.explanation: The security checklist calls for restricting both endpoints because API server exposure controls leave kubelet reachability independent.

cards.statement: A tenant permitted to create Pods and Services with externalIPs can intercept traffic aimed at those IPs.
cards.explanation: Service externalIPs can redirect traffic from other Pods or nodes, making unrestricted tenant use dangerous.

source.title: Kubernetes security advisory: ExternalIPs traffic interception

cards.statement: etcd trusting a dedicated client CA rejects certificates rooted in the separate general cluster CA.
cards.explanation: A unique etcd CA narrows datastore client trust, separating it from certificates issued under the general cluster CA.

cards.statement: A different-release checksum satisfies kubectl's integrity-check prerequisites when architectures match.
cards.explanation: A kubectl checksum must correspond to the downloaded binary's release and architecture.
cards.misconception: Architecture matching makes release matching unnecessary.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

cards.statement: A Kubernetes package verifier checks the signing key's fingerprint before trusting a newly presented key.
cards.explanation: The installation guide identifies package signing keys by fingerprint; a displayed key name provides insufficient evidence of key identity.

source.title: Install and Set Up kubectl on Linux

cards.statement: A matching SHA-256 checksum authenticates kubectl's publisher when an attacker supplies the binary and checksum.
cards.explanation: An attacker can replace both bytes and checksum; publisher authentication needs verification anchored in a trusted signer.
cards.misconception: Matching attacker-supplied hashes proves publisher identity.

cards.statement: Kubernetes v1.35 documents separate signing identities for downloaded binaries and control-plane images.
cards.explanation: The documented binary and image verification examples trust different release identities; use the identity published for that artifact class.
cards.volatilityNote: Release signer identities belong to a beta artifact-publication process and can change.

cards.statement: Verifying a signed Kubernetes SPDX document also verifies a kubectl binary downloaded separately.
cards.explanation: A signature authenticates its signed artifact; verify the downloaded kubectl binary against its own signature and certificate.
cards.misconception: A release inventory signature verifies separate release binaries.

cards.statement: A namespace-wide Secret list permission can reveal object names while keeping their data hidden.
cards.explanation: Secret list responses include Secret contents, so list access exposes credentials.
cards.misconception: Listing Secrets exposes names while withholding values.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: RBAC confines existing resource wildcard grants to APIs present when administrators create the binding.
cards.explanation: Resource wildcards also grant access to resource types added later.
cards.misconception: Resource wildcards capture a fixed API inventory.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: A user with create on serviceaccounts/token can obtain credentials for an existing ServiceAccount.
cards.explanation: TokenRequest creation issues credentials for the targeted account, exposing that account's permissions.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: A CSR creator authorized to approve kubernetes.io/kube-apiserver-client can obtain another user's API credentials.
cards.explanation: CSR creation plus authority to approve the Kubernetes API client signer can yield a certificate bearing another user's identity.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: Removing a user's RBAC bindings can revoke access conferred by system:masters membership.
cards.explanation: system:masters bypasses RBAC checks, so removing bindings leaves its superuser access intact.
cards.misconception: Binding removal revokes system:masters access.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: Users who control admission webhooks can read matched payloads beyond their own object-read grants.
cards.explanation: Configured webhooks receive matching admission objects, granting their operators visibility beyond ordinary object-read permissions.

source.title: Role Based Access Control Good Practices

cards.statement: A Pod's automountServiceAccountToken: false setting can revoke its ServiceAccount's RBAC permissions.
cards.explanation: Disabling token automount reduces automatic credential exposure; it leaves the account's authorization grants intact.
cards.misconception: Automount settings revoke account permissions.

cards.statement: Privileging a namespace's default ServiceAccount exposes Pods that omit an explicit account.
cards.explanation: Kubernetes assigns such Pods the namespace's default account, extending shared privileges to those workloads.

cards.statement: Deleting a namespace's default ServiceAccount disables default account assignment for future Pods.
cards.explanation: The control plane recreates a deleted default ServiceAccount, so deletion fails to provide a durable assignment control.
cards.misconception: Deleting the default account disables future default assignment.

cards.statement: An offline OIDC validator treats a deleted Pod's bound token as valid until that token expires.
cards.explanation: Offline OIDC validation lacks live object-existence checks; a bound token can remain accepted after its Pod is deleted.
